passage:
January: After failing her first year and barely leaving her room in Shillong, Vinita started going to Lalremsiami's free Saturday meditation class at the community hall. Lalremsiami remembered her name, noticed when she missed a week, and once walked her home in the rain. By spring Vinita was sleeping better and back in lectures.
June: At a Saturday class, Lalremsiami told the group that medicine for low moods was 'weakness'. Vinita's cousin took tablets from her doctor and was doing well. Vinita felt a jolt. She loved this teacher. She said nothing.
July: Vinita stayed back after class, heart thudding. 'Ma'am, you helped me more than anyone this year. I'm so grateful. But my cousin's medicine helped her too. I don't think it's weakness.' Lalremsiami looked surprised, then nodded slowly. 'Maybe I said that badly.' Vinita kept coming on Saturdays. She also kept thinking for herself.

qa.q: Where was Lalremsiami's meditation class held?
qa.a: The class was held at the community hall.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel in June when Lalremsiami called medicine weakness?
qa.a: Vinita felt a jolt of unease, torn because she loved this teacher.

qa.q: How did Vinita hold gratitude and clear eyes together?
qa.a: She thanked Lalremsiami sincerely and still said respectfully that she disagreed, then kept attending while thinking for herself.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami respond to being questioned?
qa.a: Lalremsiami is surprised but open, admitting she may have said it badly.

grounding: Shows deep thanks to a teacher who helped through a dark year, and Vinita keeping clear eyes by respectfully questioning one teaching.

passage: Nikita, you worry that questioning your teacher means you're ungrateful. Let your Tejas-kaka tell you about Swami Anandji. I was twenty, and my father had just died. I couldn't eat or study. Anandji ran a small ashram school near Nashik, and he let me sit in the library every afternoon, no questions asked, and fed me khichdi. He saved that year for me. I'd have done anything for him. Two years later he told us all to vote for a certain candidate, because 'the ashram needs it'. Something in me said no. I was ashamed of even thinking it. I went to him and said, 'Swamiji, I owe you my life. But my vote I must decide myself.' He was quiet for a long time. Then he laughed and said, 'Good. I didn't teach you to be a sheep.' Not every teacher would say that. But thanks and thinking can live together, Nikita.

qa.q: What did Anandji feed Tejas?
qa.a: Anandji fed him khichdi.

qa.q: How did young Tejas feel when Anandji told them how to vote?
qa.a: Tejas felt uneasy and ashamed, torn between deep gratitude and his own judgement.

qa.q: What turning point in the story shows gratitude and clear thinking together?
qa.a: Tejas telling Anandji he owed him his life but would decide his vote himself.

qa.q: How did Anandji react to Tejas's refusal?
qa.a: Anandji was quiet, then laughed and said he hadn't taught Tejas to be a sheep, accepting the independence.

grounding: An uncle recalls deep gratitude to a teacher who carried him through grief, and learning that thanks need not mean never questioning.

passage: At the yoga centre in Rishikesh where Pooja had volunteered every summer since she was eighteen, the teacher preached simple living: one meal a day, no possessions. Then Lalit, a fellow volunteer, showed her photos he had found in the office: the teacher's private villa in Goa, a foreign car, papers from a trust nobody had heard of. Pooja sat down on the office floor. For three days she felt as if someone had died. She was angry enough to throw her yoga mat in the Ganga and dismiss kindness, honesty, all of it, as a sham. On the fourth morning she woke at five out of habit, unrolled the mat on her hostel floor and did the breathing practice anyway. It still calmed her. The teacher had lied; the breath hadn't. She wrote down what she still believed: be honest, live simply, be kind. Then she told the centre she wouldn't volunteer again, and gave the photos to the trust's board.

qa.q: Where was the teacher's private villa?
qa.a: The teacher's private villa was in Goa.

qa.q: What did Pooja feel for the three days after seeing the photos?
qa.a: Pooja felt grief, as if someone had died, and enough anger to reject every value.

qa.q: How did Pooja separate the practice from the person?
qa.a: She kept doing the breathing practice and wrote down the values she still held, while leaving the centre and reporting to the board.

qa.q: Why might Lalit have shown Pooja the photos?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt she deserved to know the truth about the teacher she trusted.

grounding: Shows heartbreak on discovering a teacher's hidden luxury, grieving the image, and keeping the practice and values while leaving the person.

passage:
Dear Vijay,
You were right to be careful about the centre, and I was wrong to call you cynical.
Last week a former monk showed me the accounts: the donations we gave for the school in Ladakh went to a flat in Delhi and a car for the teacher. And there's more he wouldn't say. I cried for two days. It felt like grief, like losing a parent.
Part of me wanted to burn everything: my prayer beads, my notes, even the idea that compassion matters. I sat with the beads in my hand at 3 a.m. and couldn't do it. What I learned there about sitting with pain and being kind to people wasn't his. It was true before him.
So I'm keeping the practice and leaving the centre. I've written to the other volunteers about the accounts. I'd like to talk to you properly about all of it. Would you come for momos on Sunday?
Dolma

qa.q: Where did the donations for the school go?
qa.a: The donations went to a flat in Delhi and a car for the teacher.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel after learning the truth?
qa.a: Dolma felt grief, like losing a parent, and an urge to throw everything away in anger.

qa.q: What did Dolma decide to keep, and what to leave?
qa.a: To keep the practice and the lessons about compassion, and to leave the centre and warn the other volunteers.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Vijay may feel sad for Dolma and glad to be trusted again, happy to meet for momos.

grounding: A letter shows grief at a teacher's secret luxury, and Dolma keeping the truths learned while separating the practice from the person.

passage: Every choice, I used to text my teacher first. I'm Eshaan, and at twenty I asked him which elective to take, whether to go to my cousin's wedding, even which shirt colour was 'auspicious' for an interview. He always answered. It felt like safety. Then he went on a two-month silent retreat, no phone, and I froze. I couldn't choose a project topic. I skipped my friend Darshan's birthday because I couldn't decide on a gift. Darshan came over anyway and found me staring at my phone. 'What would you pick,' he asked, 'if nobody could tell you?' I didn't know. So he made me practise. Small things. What to eat. Which bus. Which project, with a list of pros and cons. Every choice I made alone, I wrote in a notebook. By the time my teacher came back, there were forty-one entries. I still respect him. I just ask him about big things now, and I decide.

qa.q: How long was the teacher's silent retreat?
qa.a: The silent retreat lasted two months.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when the teacher went silent?
qa.a: Eshaan felt lost and frozen, unable to make even small choices.

qa.q: What helped Eshaan build independent judgement?
qa.a: Practising small choices alone with Darshan's push and recording each one in a notebook.

qa.q: What was Darshan's view of Eshaan's dependence?
qa.a: Darshan saw that Eshaan had stopped trusting Eshaan's own judgement, and helped Eshaan practise deciding.

grounding: A spoken account of asking a teacher before every decision, feeling lost without him, and rebuilding judgement through small choices made alone.

passage:
Monday: Harsha phoned Keerthana-amma, the teacher at the Bengaluru meditation circle, three times before noon: whether to accept the internship, whether to eat before the interview, whether his dream about a snake was a sign. She answered the first. On the second she paused.
Wednesday: When he called again, she said, 'Harsha, I won't answer this one. Which do you think?' He felt a rush of panic, as if the floor had tilted. He sat on the bus-stop bench for twenty minutes. Then he chose the evening shift, because it let him keep his morning classes.
Saturday: At the circle, she asked him how the shift was going. 'Fine,' he said, surprised. 'I chose it.' She smiled. 'A guide who makes all your choices isn't guiding you anywhere. Keep choosing the small things. Bring me only the ones that keep you awake.' That night Harsha decided, alone, to call his mother on Sundays instead of Fridays.

qa.q: How many times did Harsha phone Keerthana-amma before noon on Monday?
qa.a: Harsha phoned her three times before noon.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel when Keerthana-amma refused to answer?
qa.a: Harsha felt a rush of panic, as if the floor had tilted.

qa.q: Why is Keerthana-amma's approach that of a good guide?
qa.a: She stops answering small questions so Harsha builds his own judgement, and asks him to bring only the big ones.

qa.q: What does Keerthana-amma want for Harsha?
qa.a: She wants him to trust his own judgement rather than depend on her for every choice.

grounding: Shows a young man who asks his teacher before every choice, and a good guide stepping back so he learns he can decide small things alone.

passage: I'm Manoj, and last year my closest friend Satish moved into an ashram in the hills and stopped answering his family. His sister Pooja called me crying: 'He won't take Amma's calls. Please do something.' My first instinct was to storm up there and tell him the guru was a fraud and he had to choose: us or them. I even typed it. Then I remembered how he got when his father used to shout; he'd dig in harder. So I went up on a Sunday with his favourite chikki and just sat with him on the steps. I asked him what he loved about it. He talked for an hour: the silence, the early mornings, feeling useful. I didn't argue. At the end I said, 'Your Amma misses your voice. Would you call her, even once?' He was quiet. I visit every month now. Last month he called his mother. It's slow. But the door's still open.

qa.q: What did Manoj bring Satish?
qa.a: Manoj brought Satish his favourite chikki.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when Pooja called crying?
qa.a: Manoj felt worried and angry, tempted to storm up and give Satish an ultimatum.

qa.q: Why was sitting and asking questions better than an ultimatum?
qa.a: Satish digs in when pushed, so staying warm and curious kept the door open and led to him calling his mother.

qa.q: What is it like for Pooja when Satish won't take calls?
qa.a: Pooja is distressed and helpless, crying as she asks Manoj to do something.

grounding: A first-person account of worrying about a friend who cut off his family for an ashram, and staying warm and curious instead of attacking his teacher.

passage: Note from Mehak, faculty mentor, Thursday. Wasim from my second-year tutorial group asked to talk after class. His first-year roommate, Arif, has moved into a spiritual community outside the city and has blocked his parents' numbers. Wasim was clearly anxious; he kept twisting his watch strap. He said he had planned to send Arif a long message listing everything wrong with the group's leader and telling him to come back or forget their friendship. I asked what he thought Arif would do with that message. Wasim said, 'Block me too, probably.' We talked about staying in touch without attacking what Arif values: small, warm messages, asking about his days, letting him know Wasim is there whenever he wants to talk. Wasim decided to send a photo from their old hostel room instead, with 'Miss our chai. Here whenever.' I suggested he also let Arif's parents know he's in contact. I'll follow up next week.

qa.q: What did Wasim decide to send Arif?
qa.a: Wasim decided to send a photo from their old hostel room with 'Miss our chai. Here whenever.'

qa.q: What does Wasim twisting his watch strap suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Wasim is anxious and worried about Arif.

qa.q: Why is a warm message wiser than the long critical one?
qa.a: Attacking the leader would likely make Arif block Wasim too; staying warm keeps the door open.

qa.q: How might Arif react to a message attacking his group's leader?
qa.a: Arif would probably feel attacked and cut Wasim off, as Wasim himself guesses.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a student worried about a friend who cut off his family for a spiritual group, choosing warmth and curiosity over an ultimatum.

passage: Salma, you say the new group at college feeds you every evening and calls you family. That's lovely. Let your Chetan-uncle tell you about 1990. I came to Chennai at nineteen, knew no one, and spent a whole year eating alone. Then some young men from a 'self-improvement' circle invited me in. The first week was like a festival: dinners, hugs, people saying 'you belong here'. I felt warm for the first time in months. By the third week, the warmth had rules. Miss a meeting and nobody spoke to you. Visit your family and you were 'going backwards'. I noticed because my cousin's wedding came up, and the love vanished the moment I said I'd go. So I went, and I didn't go back. Enjoy their kindness, Salma. Just watch whether it stays when you say no to something.

qa.q: How long did Chetan eat alone after coming to Chennai?
qa.a: Chetan ate alone for a whole year.

qa.q: How did young Chetan feel during the first week with the circle?
qa.a: Chetan felt warm and welcome for the first time in months after a lonely year.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed Chetan the warmth had conditions?
qa.a: Saying he would go to his cousin's wedding, after which the love vanished.

qa.q: How did the circle's members treat people who missed meetings?
qa.a: They stopped speaking to them, treating absence as disloyalty.

grounding: An uncle recalls a group's flood of warmth after a lonely year, and noticing the love was tied to obedience and cutting off family.

passage: It was Vaibhav's first week in Hyderabad, monsoon rain every afternoon, and he had eaten dinner alone for six nights when a group from the 'Light Circle' found him at the bus stop and offered a ride. For the next five days they fed him, texted him every morning, and said, 'You were meant to find us.' He felt warm for the first time since leaving home. On the sixth day the leader asked him to skip his cousin Salma's visit that weekend for a 'deeper retreat'. 'Family can wait,' the leader said, smiling. Vaibhav felt a small cold spot under the warmth. He texted Salma, who had been in the city two years: 'They're so kind, but they don't want me to meet you.' She replied at once: 'Kindness that asks you to drop your family isn't kindness. Keep our Saturday. You can still be friendly with them.' Vaibhav kept Saturday. The group's texts dropped from ten a day to none.

qa.q: How many nights had Vaibhav eaten alone before the group found him?
qa.a: Vaibhav had eaten alone for six nights.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav feel when the leader asked him to skip Salma's visit?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt a small cold spot of unease under the warmth.

qa.q: What did Salma's advice help Vaibhav notice?
qa.a: That kindness tied to dropping family is a warning sign, so he kept Saturday while staying friendly.

qa.q: What does the group's sudden silence suggest?
qa.a: It suggests their warmth depended on obedience, and faded when Vaibhav chose his family.

grounding: Shows a lonely newcomer showered with attention, then asked to skip family, and noticing the kindness was tied to cutting others off.

passage: The group met in a farmhouse outside Sangrur, and Gurleen had gone every Sunday for two months. The singing was lovely and people were kind. Then, at the last meeting, the leader collected everyone's phones in a basket 'for the evening's growth'. Later he spoke about donating 'what you can, and then a little more', and said old friends who 'mock the path' should be left behind. Gurleen thought of Avni, who had once laughed at the white clothes. Walking home along the canal, she felt her chest tighten. Her savings for the teacher-training course were in her account. She called Avni from the bus stand. 'I think they want my phone, my money and my friends,' she said, and it sounded worse aloud. Avni didn't laugh. 'Keep your phone. Don't give anything. And take the 6 o'clock bus home next Sunday; I'll wait at the stop.' Gurleen agreed. She gave nothing the next week.

qa.q: What did the leader collect in a basket?
qa.a: The leader collected everyone's phones.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel walking home along the canal?
qa.a: Gurleen felt uneasy, her chest tightening, worried about her savings and her friends.

qa.q: What steps kept Gurleen safer?
qa.a: Keeping her phone and money, talking to Avni outside the group, and planning a set time home with Avni waiting.

qa.q: How does Avni respond to Gurleen's call?
qa.a: Avni takes it seriously, doesn't laugh, and offers practical support.

grounding: Shows a leader asking for phones, donations and cutting off friends 'for growth', and Gurleen reading these as control signals and talking to a friend outside.

passage: In his first winter at university in Stockholm, Emeka joined a Thursday 'leadership circle' that met in a warm flat full of candles. Anders, who ran it, was charming and quick to praise. After a month, the requests started. 'Serious members hand in their phones during weekend retreats.' Then: 'Your contribution shows your commitment.' Then, gently: 'Your old friends from the Nigerian students' society hold you back.' Emeka noticed he had stopped going to the society's Friday dinners. That frightened him. He thought of his cousin in Lagos, who always said, 'Never give anyone your only way home.' So before the next retreat he told Anders he would keep his phone. He kept his savings in his own account. And on Friday he went to the society dinner and told his friend Tunde everything. Tunde listened and said, 'Come to dinner every Friday. If they don't like that, you'll know.'

qa.q: When did the Nigerian students' society have dinners?
qa.a: The society had dinners on Fridays.

qa.q: What did Emeka feel on noticing he had stopped going to the society dinners?
qa.a: Emeka felt frightened, realising how far he had drifted from old friends.

qa.q: What did Emeka keep to protect himself?
qa.a: His phone, his own savings and his friendships, and he told Tunde, someone outside the group.

qa.q: How does Anders frame his requests?
qa.a: Anders frames them as commitment and growth, so control sounds like a gift.

grounding: Shows a charming leader asking for phones, money and distance from old friends, and Emeka keeping independent contact, money and a way out.

passage: When Aiko said the 'mindful living' group sounded strange, Gabriel defended it hard. 'They saved me when I first came to Tokyo. You don't know them.' They were sitting in a ramen shop near the university, and his voice was louder than he meant. The truth was, doubts had been growing for months. The group discouraged reading anything the leader hadn't approved. Members who asked about the fees were called 'unready'. Last week he had wanted to ask why, and hadn't. Now, defending them to Aiko, he heard phrases he had been taught coming out of his own mouth. On the train home he opened his notes and wrote a list titled 'Questions I'm not allowed to ask'. There were seven. He stared at it. Loyalty that forbids thinking, he realised, was a strange kind of loyalty. The next day he messaged Aiko: 'Sorry I snapped. Can I show you a list?'

qa.q: How many questions were on Gabriel's list?
qa.a: There were seven questions on the list.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling while defending the group to Aiko?
qa.a: Gabriel felt defensive and loyal while privately doubting, which made his voice louder than he meant.

qa.q: Why was writing the list a wise step?
qa.a: It made the forbidden questions visible, helping Gabriel examine his loyalty instead of silencing his doubts.

qa.q: How might Aiko have felt when Gabriel snapped?
qa.a: Aiko may have felt hurt and worried, since she had only said the group sounded strange.

grounding: Shows loyal defence of a group despite growing private doubts, and Gabriel noticing the questions he is not allowed to ask.

passage: In the girls' hostel common room in Manipal, Seema was defending the 'Awakening Circle' again. 'They're the only people who get me,' she told Anjali. 'You just don't understand.' Anjali didn't argue. She asked one question: 'What happens if someone in the circle disagrees with the leader?' Seema opened her mouth to answer and found she didn't know. Nobody ever had, not out loud. There was the girl who asked about the fees in March and stopped being invited. Seema had told herself that girl wasn't serious. That night, on the top bunk, Seema made a list of things she wanted to ask the leader and hadn't dared: where the money went, why they couldn't read other books, why members had to recruit two friends. Her stomach tightened with each line. She missed the warmth already, just thinking about it. But the next Sunday, she asked the first question.

qa.q: What question did Anjali ask?
qa.a: Anjali asked, 'What happens if someone in the circle disagrees with the leader?'

qa.q: What did Seema feel as she wrote the list?
qa.a: Seema felt her stomach tighten with fear and a sense of loss, already missing the warmth.

qa.q: What did Seema do that tested her loyalty honestly?
qa.a: She listed the questions she hadn't dared ask and then asked the first one.

qa.q: Why might Anjali have asked a question instead of arguing?
qa.a: Anjali probably knew arguing would make Seema defensive, while a question would let her think.

grounding: Shows a student defending a group out of belonging while doubts grow, and a friend's question helping her notice what she is not allowed to ask.

passage: Hemant had come home to Kolkata for Durga Puja only because the group allowed a three-day visit. By the second evening, his elder brother Anirban had had enough. 'You've given them your scholarship money, you don't call Ma, you talk like a recording. Please, just leave them.' Hemant felt the familiar heat. The group had warned him: family would try to pull him back into 'the lower life'. They were the enemy of his growth. He stood up to leave. Then, at the door, he saw Ma in the kitchen, not crying, just holding the ladle very still, staring at nothing. The look went through him. It wasn't anger. It was fear, and underneath, love. He came back and sat down. 'I'm not leaving the group tonight,' he told Anirban. 'But I'll call Ma every Sunday. I promise that.' Anirban swallowed. 'That's something.' On Sunday, back at the group, Hemant stepped outside at eight and called home.

qa.q: How long a visit had the group allowed?
qa.a: The group had allowed a three-day visit.

qa.q: What did Hemant feel on seeing Ma's stillness?
qa.a: Hemant felt moved, sensing fear and, underneath it, love.

qa.q: What did Hemant do that kept a connection alive?
qa.a: He promised to call Ma every Sunday and kept that promise even back at the group.

qa.q: How does Anirban see the group?
qa.a: Anirban sees it as taking Hemant's money and his voice, and wants him out.

grounding: Shows a young man who sees his pleading family as enemies, hearing the love inside their fear, and keeping one connection alive.

passage: Anand's mother, Yamini, stood outside the group's shared flat in Pune with a steel tiffin of his favourite rajma. The member who opened the door said Anand was 'in reflection' and couldn't come down. Yamini waited on the stairs for an hour. When Anand finally came, he stood two steps above her, arms folded. 'The teacher says your worry is attachment. You're trying to pull me backwards.' Yamini's voice broke. 'I'm not your enemy, beta. I only want to see you eat.' Anand felt something crack under his folded arms. He had been told she would say that, that it was a trick. But her hands were shaking as she held the tiffin, and no trick made hands shake like that. He came down one step and took the tiffin. 'I'm not coming home, Ma. But you can come every Saturday. I'll come down.' She nodded, wiping her face. He ate the rajma that night, alone in his room, slowly.

qa.q: What did Yamini bring in the tiffin?
qa.a: Yamini brought Anand's favourite rajma.

qa.q: What did Anand feel when he saw Yamini's shaking hands?
qa.a: Anand felt something crack, moved by her love despite being told her worry was a trick.

qa.q: What connection did Anand choose to keep?
qa.a: Letting his mother visit every Saturday and coming down to see her.

qa.q: What does Yamini want, in her own words?
qa.a: Only to see Anand eat, which shows the love behind her fear.

grounding: Shows a young man told to treat his fearful mother as an enemy, seeing the love inside her fear and keeping a weekly connection.

passage: My name is Chinmay, and I spent three years in a group that promised to 'build a new society of truth'. We sold their books door to door, lived in shared rooms, gave our stipends. The leader said money didn't matter. Then I saw his new house. I left within a week. The first month out, I felt like the biggest fool alive. Three years, gone. I had missed my grandmother's last birthday. I couldn't stop replaying every time I'd ignored a doubt. My old school friend Lalit came to get me on his bike. He didn't say 'I told you so', though he had. He said, 'Leaving took guts. Most people stay.' He found me a counsellor at the university clinic who had worked with former members of groups. It's been six months. I'm back in class, I visit my grandmother's friends, and some days I still grieve. But I'm learning to say 'I was deceived,' not 'I was stupid.'

qa.q: How long was Chinmay in the group?
qa.a: Chinmay was in the group for three years.

qa.q: What did Chinmay feel in the first month after leaving?
qa.a: Chinmay felt foolish and full of grief over the lost years.

qa.q: What helped Chinmay rebuild?
qa.a: Lalit's support, a counsellor who knew former members, and slowly returning to class and old ties.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Chinmay's leaving?
qa.a: Lalit sees it as brave, saying leaving took guts when most people stay.

grounding: A first-person account of seeing a group's promises betrayed by its actions, grieving lost years, and rebuilding with support and counselling instead of self-blame.

passage: Counsellor's note, Kashish, student support office, Monday. Bhavna, final-year BSc, came for her third session. She left a campus 'mentorship' group in August after two years, when she learned the leader had been spending member contributions on himself. Today she said, 'I can't forgive myself. I was so stupid. Everyone else saw it.' She had stopped going to lectures because she felt people were laughing at her. I told her plainly that groups like this are skilled at drawing in bright, caring people, and that leaving was a brave act, not a foolish one. We named what the two years had also given her: friends she still trusts, a talent for organising. We set small steps: attend two lectures this week, call her aunt on Wednesday, and consider the support circle for former members on Thursday evenings. She agreed to the first two and will think about the third. Next session: Friday.

qa.q: When did Bhavna leave the group?
qa.a: Bhavna left in August, after two years.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling about herself?
qa.a: Bhavna felt ashamed and full of self-blame, calling herself stupid and imagining people laughing.

qa.q: What small steps did Kashish and Bhavna agree on?
qa.a: Attending two lectures, calling her aunt on Wednesday, and considering the Thursday support circle for former members.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Bhavna's leaving?
qa.a: Kashish sees it as brave, and the group as skilled at drawing in bright, caring people.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a former member's self-blame after leaving a group, reframed as courage, with support and slow rebuilding.

passage: The overnight train to Goa was stuck outside Ratnagiri for three hours, and Manjula, heading back from a group retreat, couldn't stop crying quietly into her dupatta. The woman in the opposite berth, Maria, handed her a biscuit and waited. Eventually Manjula told her: the retreat, the leader's anger when she asked to go home for her father's birthday, the fear of what would happen if she left. Maria nodded slowly. 'I was in a group like that for four years. I was scared of the same things. The leader said my family would suffer if I left.' 'Did they?' 'No. I did, for a while. Now I'm mostly at peace.' Manjula waited for Maria to tell her what to do. She didn't. 'You don't have to decide on this train,' Maria said. 'Maybe just one step. Maybe your father's birthday.' When the train moved, they swapped numbers. Manjula texted her father: 'Coming for your birthday.'

qa.q: How long was the train stuck outside Ratnagiri?
qa.a: The train was stuck for three hours.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling on the train?
qa.a: Manjula felt frightened and upset, crying quietly about the leader's anger and what leaving might bring.

qa.q: What makes Maria's help wise?
qa.a: She shares her experience, listens, and suggests one safe step without telling Manjula what to decide.

qa.q: How does Maria relate to Manjula's fears?
qa.a: Maria felt the same fears during four years in a similar group, and now mostly finds peace.

grounding: Shows a former member sharing that she felt the same fears and found peace, helping Manjula feel less alone and take one step without being told what to do.

passage: Sabina had been in the 'Inner Light' group for eighteen months when she noticed Hansa at a café near Bandra station. Hansa had left the group a year ago; the leader said she had 'fallen'. Sabina nearly walked past. Instead she sat down. Hansa didn't lecture. She talked about her first months out: the nightmares, the guilt, the relief of reading any book she wanted. 'I was scared of exactly what you're scared of,' she said. 'That I'd be nothing without them.' Sabina felt her throat close. For the first time in months she felt less alone. 'So what should I do?' Hansa shook her head. 'I'm not going to be your new leader. Don't swap one person telling you what to do for another. But if you want, come to the Tuesday meeting for former members. Just listen.' Sabina didn't promise. But she saved the address, and on the way home she called her mother for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: Where did Sabina see Hansa?
qa.a: Sabina saw Hansa at a café near Bandra station.

qa.q: What did Sabina feel as Hansa spoke?
qa.a: Sabina felt less alone for the first time in months, her throat closing with emotion.

qa.q: Why does Hansa refuse to tell Sabina what to do?
qa.a: So Sabina doesn't swap one authority for another, and can take her own steps at her own pace.

qa.q: How does Hansa describe her time since leaving?
qa.a: Hansa describes nightmares and guilt at first, then relief, like reading any book she wants.

grounding: Shows a former member sharing her own fears and peace, and refusing to become a new authority, so Sabina can take one step at a time.
